notes: Locomotor planning and gait modification rest on a cortical division of labor: posterior parietal cortex builds an estimate of the animal's position relative to objects in its path to plan visually guided locomotion, while motor cortex executes gait modifications by phasically modulating groups of synergistic muscles active at different times in the gait cycle.
animal_study: Transiently inactivate PPC versus motor cortex during visually guided locomotion over obstacles while recording EMG of synergistic muscle groups, to test the claimed dissociation between planning (PPC) and phase-locked execution (motor cortex).
robot_sim: Add a supraspinal layer to a CPG walker in which a PPC-like module estimates body-to-obstacle geometry for planning and a motor-cortex-like module phase-gates muscle synergies; ablating each module should selectively degrade obstacle negotiation versus flat-ground gait modification.

notes: Diffusive voltage coupling between nonlinear neural oscillators can dephase rather than synchronize them, producing a bursting-like regime in which oscillators synchronize at small oscillation amplitude and desynchronize once amplitude grows large — a mechanism by which coupling structure alone generates antiphase and amplitude switching in oscillator pairs.
robot_sim: Couple half-center or inter-leg CPG oscillators diffusively in the voltage variable and sweep coupling strength and amplitude to check for dephasing and amplitude-switching bursts; relevant whenever naive diffusive coupling is assumed to be synchronizing.

notes: Proposes 'learning to stop' — endowing locomotion controllers with the ability to halt safely — as a unifying principle for locomotion in varying environments: a deep deterministic policy gradient agent with the stop capability transfers controllers from water to land quickly and safely, plausibly modeling how locomotion strategies crossed the water-to-land transition.
animal_study: In an amphibious animal model, quantify stopping behavior and recovery from destabilization during initial water-to-land locomotor experience to test whether stopping competence accompanies newly transferred locomotion strategies, as the learning-to-stop hypothesis predicts.
robot_sim: Train DDPG locomotion controllers with and without an explicit stop action in water and land simulations and compare transfer success, training safety, and recovery from destabilization across environments.

notes: Focal alpha2-noradrenergic action at restricted lumbar levels both starts and stops spinal walking: topical clonidine over L3-L4 or L5-L7, or microinjection at L3-L5, induces treadmill locomotion in acutely spinalized cats, whereas yohimbine at L3-L5 (not L6) or a transection at L3-L4 blocks it — mid-lumbar segments are a sufficient pharmacological trigger and a necessary substrate for the rhythm.
animal_study: Combine segment-restricted clonidine/yohimbine application with selective deafferentation or graded sensory perturbations to test how mid-lumbar rhythmogenesis interacts with afferent gating; alternatively test in chronic preparations whether repeated L3-L4 noradrenergic stimulation enhances recovery of stepping.
robot_sim: Build a spatially segmented spinal CPG in which only mid-lumbar-equivalent modules can be tonically activated to launch the full hindlimb pattern; ablating those modules while leaving caudal motoneuron pools functional should abolish gait but spare other rhythmic outputs.

notes: Frames vertebrate locomotor control as spinal CPG microcircuits setting muscle timing with sensory compensation for perturbations, brainstem command systems setting CPG activity level and locomotor speed, basal ganglia selecting and initiating/stopping motor programs, with postural and steering systems integrated around the propulsive core.
animal_study: Use the framework's level structure to design dissociation experiments — brainstem stimulation during spinal CPG recordings to map speed control, or basal ganglia manipulation during gait initiation and stopping — to test the predicted hierarchy of command, selection, and pattern generation.
robot_sim: Architect a controller with distinct CPG modules, brainstem-like drive/gain modules for speed, and a basal ganglia-like action-selection layer that starts and stops locomotion; ablate each level to reproduce the framework's predicted functional dissociations.

notes: Rapid plantar flexion perturbations in late stance transiently suppress soleus EMG in proportion to treadmill inclination and Achilles tendon force (not ankle kinematics), indicating that Golgi tendon organ feedback via the group Ib pathway operates as positive force feedback enhancing ankle extensor activity during late stance of human walking.
animal_study: In an instrumented animal walking preparation with tendon force and Ib afferent recording, apply matched late-stance unloading perturbations across inclines to measure the gain and phase dependence of the positive force feedback loop.
robot_sim: Implement stance-gated positive force feedback from tendon-force-like Ib signals onto ankle extensor motoneurons in a neuromuscular walker and ablate it: the model should lose inclination-dependent late-stance extensor enhancement and show the unload-induced EMG drop.

notes: Spinal 5-HT7 receptor blockade (not 5-HT2A) in adult rats reorganizes recovery quadrupedal locomotion into a transiently stable 2:1 forelimb-to-hindlimb stepping pattern, implicating lamina VII 5-HT7-expressing interneurons with ascending projections in setting fore-hindlimb coupling.
animal_study: Silence or ablate lamina VII 5-HT7-positive ascending interneurons, or apply SB269970 selectively rostral versus caudal to a spinal transection, to localize where the 2FL-1HL coupling is generated and confirm the receptor-subclass specificity.
robot_sim: Model fore-hindlimb coupling through an ascending serotonergic-modulated interneuron path between hindlimb and forelimb CPGs; removing the 5-HT7-like gain should lock the network into a 2:1 forelimb-to-hindlimb pattern.

notes: A tractable model of mouse locomotion — four per-limb state-machine rhythm generators with limb load, extension, and balance feedback — separates the roles of sensory feedback from central propriospinal interactions in speed-dependent gait expression, and predicts that postural imbalance feedback critically controls swing-to-stance transitions and stabilization of walking direction.
animal_study: Perturb limb loading or balance (lateral support shifts, single-limb loading) at defined speeds in walking mice and measure inter-limb phase and swing-to-stance timing to test whether transition timing shifts as the model predicts.
robot_sim: Implement four per-limb rhythm generators with load-, extension-, and balance-driven state transitions; ablate the balance signal to test for destabilized swing-to-stance transitions and wandering direction, and ablate propriospinal inter-limb coupling to reproduce speed-dependent gait changes.
flags: Postural-imbalance feedback controlling swing-to-stance transitions and walking direction has no Feedback vocabulary entry — consider proposing one. Near-identical bioRxiv preprint (2023) appears in this batch as recFqSV9WOXZsTiV9 — dedupe candidate.

notes: Vertical body oscillation during self-paced running clusters at 2.7-2.8 Hz, matching dominant frequencies of heart rate and of runners' preferred music, with EEG delta power rising after running — supporting the speculation that a common ~3 Hz oscillator, possibly a locomotor central pattern generator, couples intrinsic and extrinsic rhythms during exercise.
animal_study: Record locomotor, autonomic, and cortical rhythms concurrently in running animals before and after spinal transection to test whether the ~3 Hz coupling survives spinalization, which would localize the shared oscillator to a spinal CPG as speculated.
robot_sim: Embed a CPG in a neuromechanical running model driving coupled oscillator loads representing autonomic and cortical-like subsystems, and test frequency locking to the locomotor rhythm under speed changes.

notes: Running turns in bipeds are constrained by matching body rotation to movement direction: humans generate large braking forces to prevent over-rotation whereas ostriches obtain appropriate rotation from lateral force alone (aided by greater rotational inertia relative to body mass), humans stabilize orientation within the theoretical two-step minimum, and horizontal-plane leg forces follow spring-mass behavior — so passive dynamic stabilization contributes to maneuver stability.
animal_study: Record 3D kinetics and kinematics of turning in bipedal species spanning rotational-inertia ratios to test the rotation-matching model's prediction that braking requirements scale with rotational inertia relative to body mass.
robot_sim: Implement a biped with horizontal-plane spring-mass legs and a rotation-matching turn controller; verify that fore-aft braking against over-rotation emerges and that increasing rotational inertia removes the braking requirement, reproducing the human-versus-ostrich contrast.
flags: Ostriches are discussed as the comparison biped but are not in the animals vocabulary.

notes: In a closed-loop neuromechanical model of insect joint control, slow muscle fibers act as temporal integrators of sensory feedback that improve limb positioning accuracy, and common inhibitory motor neurons reset this integration by accelerating muscle relaxation at commanded position changes — allowing stance-phase speed control independent of swing amplitude or duration through the gain of sensory feedback to stance muscles.
animal_study: Record common inhibitor activity and slow fiber responses in walking insects while manipulating stance load or commanded position, to test whether CI firing accelerates relaxation at position changes and whether stance speed is set by proprioceptive feedback gain.
robot_sim: Give simulated joint actuators slow-fiber (leaky-integrator) dynamics with sensory feedback plus a CI-like inhibitory reset input; ablating CI should slow relaxation after retargeting, and raising stance feedback gain should speed stance without altering swing amplitude or duration.
flags: Core mechanism is efferent (common inhibitor MN plus slow-fiber dynamics), so no afferent Feedback vocabulary entry applies.

notes: A two-legged neuromuscular model shows that intrinsic muscle stiffness driven by a stereotyped rhythmic pattern sustains surprisingly stable gait without sensory control, that spindle Ia and tendon organ Ib stretch-reflex feedback (35 ms latency, 30% of the EMG profile, active only when the receptor-bearing muscle contracts) is crucial for load compensation only when central drive is low, and that finite-state control greatly extends adaptive capability.
animal_study: In decerebrate or spinal walking animals with graded central drive, block spindle and tendon organ afferents to test the prediction that deafferentation destabilizes gait mainly at low levels of central activation.
robot_sim: Add state-gated autogenic Ia/Ib stretch feedback (fixed latency, bounded contribution to motoneuron activation) to a feedforward-driven Hill-muscle biped and ablate it at high versus low central drive to reproduce the state-dependent stabilizing contribution.
flags: Abstract does not name the species of the bipedal planar model (human-like slow level walking) — animals left empty. State-gated autogenic Ia/Ib reflex has no exact vocabulary entry beyond the preflexive one.

notes: In isolated neonatal mouse brainstem-spinal cord preparations, removing or cooling the brain stem increases locomotor rhythm frequency and shortens axial and hindlimb motoneuron bursts without altering the tonic excitability component, showing brainstem locomotor circuits are operational at birth and extend the operating range of spinal axial and hindlimb rhythm-generating circuits.
animal_study: Record identified brainstem neurons and silence them during fictive locomotor-like activity to determine which descending pathway sets rhythm frequency versus burst duration, and whether the modulation is segregated between axial and hindlimb circuits.
robot_sim: Add a descending module that independently scales CPG frequency and burst duration over axial and hindlimb rhythm generators; ablating it should reproduce the faster, shorter-burst rhythm observed after brain stem removal.

notes: A three-subset local neuron population model — main and auxiliary excitatory subsets plus an inhibitory subset, wired in positive and negative feedback loops — produces rhythmic activity under white-noise input in its stable regime and input-dependent limit cycles at higher mean input, with an electronic realization generating EEG-like background activity and paroxysmal spikes.
robot_sim: Use the excitatory-inhibitory population loop architecture as a building block when adding inhibitory subsets to CPG layers, sweeping input level to map stable rhythmic output versus limit-cycle regimes.

notes: In spinal cats stepping via functional electrical stimulation, an intrinsically timed controller achieves overground stepping more easily (lower sensitivity to initial stimulation parameters) but cannot compensate walkway resistance or muscle fatigue, while a sensory-driven controller that switches between unloaded flexion and loaded extension phases adapts to loading — motivating a combined controller that runs on intrinsic timing but resets phase from sensory signals.
animal_study: Compare intrinsically timed, sensory-driven, and combined FES controllers across repeated sessions in instrumented spinal cats, quantifying load-bearing stepping and adaptation to induced muscle fatigue.
robot_sim: Implement a fixed-timing CPG with load-based sensory phase resetting (combined controller) in a neuromuscular biped; ablating the sensory reset should cause failures under fatigue-like actuator force decay and changing walkway resistance, reproducing the timed controller's limitation.
flags: Sensory-driven flexion/extension phase transitions were implemented with external sensors (force plates, accelerometers) — no afferent type identified, so no Feedback vocabulary entry applies.

notes: In chronically spinalized cats, a second transection at caudal L3 or L4 permanently abolishes treadmill locomotion even after weeks of training, while lesions at L2 or rostral L3 spare it; fast paw shakes and clonidine-induced hindlimb hyperextension persist below the lesion, so mid-lumbar segments are necessary specifically for locomotor rhythm expression, not for other rhythmic motor patterns or caudal motoneuron function.
animal_study: Record from L3-L4 interneuron populations during both locomotion and paw shaking, combined with the segmental transection logic, to identify which mid-lumbar circuits are locomotion-selective; test whether electrical stimulation at L3-L4 substitutes for their disconnection.
robot_sim: Model a spatially distributed spinal network where only mid-lumbar-equivalent modules generate the locomotor pattern while caudal segments retain reflex and rhythmic capacity; ablating the mid-lumbar module should eliminate gait but leave paw-shake-like rhythmicity intact.

notes: Legged locomotion over uneven terrain is statically indeterminate and unstable under position-velocity control; directly controlling actuator forces — as in multi-fingered grasping, under an assumption of zero horizontal foot interaction forces — removes the stability problem at moderate computational cost.
robot_sim: Swap joint position-velocity control for direct force control in a legged simulator on uneven terrain and verify the predicted stability improvement and computational savings under the zero-horizontal-foot-interaction assumption.

notes: Cockroaches step at bimodally distributed slow (<10 cm/s) and fast (~30 cm/s) rates whether freely exploring or tethered on oiled glass with inter-leg mechanical coupling removed, with distinct joint-kinematic distributions per gait and a transition near a Froude number of ~0.4 — establishing multiple discrete gaits and requiring gait-aware interpretation of neural locomotor control data.
animal_study: Use the tethered oiled-plate preparation to isolate neural coupling and record motor neurons or interneurons at matched slow versus fast stepping, then manipulate load at Froude-matched conditions to probe the gait-switch mechanism.
robot_sim: Build a hexapod controller whose gait switches near Froude ~0.4 and test whether bimodal stepping and distinct joint-kinematics distributions persist when mechanical inter-leg coupling is removed, dissociating neural from mechanical gait determination.

notes: Lumbar locomotor V3 interneurons provide direct, somatotopically organized excitatory synaptic input to thoracic sympathetic preganglionic neurons (8-20% of their glutamatergic input), where optical activation evokes prolonged depolarizations or action potentials — an intraspinal route coupling locomotor activation to autonomic recruitment without supraspinal mediation.
animal_study: Silence or ablate lumbar V3 interneurons during locomotion while recording sympathetic outflow and autonomic effectors, to test whether this intraspinal pathway is necessary for movement-coupled autonomic activation.
robot_sim: Add a propriospinal excitatory branch from lumbar CPG modules to an autonomic controller layer in a neuromechanical model and ablate it to quantify the loss of locomotion-driven autonomic entrainment.
flags: Abstract does not state the species (optogenetic spinal cord and slice preparations) — animals left empty pending full text. The V3-to-SPN excitatory propriospinal pathway is not an afferent feedback pathway and has no vocabulary entry.

notes: A piecewise-linear approximation of the spring-loaded inverted pendulum — whose only nonlinearity is the stance-flight switching event — reproduces the bifurcation structure and parametric sensitivities of the nonlinear SLIP model across parameter space while providing closed-form stance trajectories and touchdown-to-touchdown stride maps that compute far faster than numerical integration.
robot_sim: Use the closed-form piecewise-linear stride map as a fast analytical plant for gait planning and stability analysis in legged-robot controllers, validating bifurcation fidelity against numerically integrated SLIP.

notes: Distills principles of insect walking for legged robots: highly distributed control, synergy of local reflexes with distributed gait control, and matching body mechanics to terrain yield robust complex-terrain locomotion with modest computational resources — while insect legs vastly exceed robots in degrees of freedom, sensory richness (hundreds of joint and stress sensors plus antennae), and actuator performance, integrating this feedback to reconfigure the legs step-by-step.
animal_study: Ablate antennal or proprioceptive inputs in walking insects across terrain changes and measure the step-by-step reconfiguration of leg degrees of freedom, to pin down the reflex-gait synergy the review proposes transferring to robots.
robot_sim: Build hexapod controllers layering distributed per-leg reflexes under distributed gait control and ablate either layer on rough terrain to test the claimed synergy and the robustness-versus-computation trade-off.

notes: Classic formulation of the principles underlying nervous control of innate rhythmic motor acts in vertebrates, establishing the in vitro lamprey spinal cord preparation in which the locomotor motor pattern can be elicited in isolated cord sections for detailed mechanism analysis, and proposing that parts of the locomotor network are reused in other motor acts, including learned ones.
animal_study: In the isolated lamprey preparation, elicit multiple motor acts and identify shared versus act-specific interneuron components to test the network-reuse hypothesis directly.
robot_sim: Implement modular CPG subnetworks shared across multiple motor programs in a simulated swimmer or walker and verify that reuse preserves timing and stability while reducing controller complexity.

notes: Lateral perturbations in the cat recruit context-specific postural mechanisms: during standing, corrective redistribution of muscle activity between symmetrical limbs (contralateral hindlimb extensor excitation with ipsilateral inhibition); during walking, a corrective lateral step whose direction depends on push timing relative to the step cycle and whose EMG signature is marked hip abductor and adductor reprogramming — reconfiguring the base of support rather than redistributing activity.
animal_study: Apply phase-controlled lateral pushes before and after deafferentation or spinal transection to determine which afferents encode the lateral perturbation and whether the corrective-step reprogramming is spinal.
robot_sim: Implement phase-dependent lateral-perturbation correction in a legged model — standing mode redistributes extensor activity across limbs, walking mode triggers a corrective lateral step via step-cycle-gated hip abductor/adductor modulation — and test recovery against push timing.
flags: Lateral-perturbation corrective responses are a postural feedback pathway with no Feedback vocabulary entry.

notes: In a human neuro-musculo-skeletal walking model, purely reflex-based control can match the perturbation stability of CPG-based models but offers no simple means of controlling speed or step length; adding a CPG feedforward component restores simple gait modulation, delineating complementary roles in which reflexes dominate stability and the CPG provides speed and step-length control.
animal_study: Test whether animals walking under graded central drive versus reflex-only conditions show the predicted dissociation — stable but speed-locked gait without modulation of central rhythmic drive.
robot_sim: Extend a reflex-based walking model with a half-center CPG feedforward module and demonstrate speed and step-length control; ablating the CPG should reproduce stable but poorly modulable gait.

notes: bioRxiv preprint of the same mouse-locomotion model paper as the published Royal Society Open Science version, which is curated in this corpus as recCjTyA6Mz9tHw0G: four per-limb state-machine rhythm generators with limb load, extension, and balance feedback, dissociating sensory feedback from central propriospinal interactions in speed-dependent gait expression and predicting that postural imbalance feedback controls swing-to-stance transitions and walking direction. The scientific summary should be cited from the published record recCjTyA6Mz9tHw0G; this preprint entry is retained for deduplication only.
animal_study: Perturb limb loading or balance (lateral support shifts, single-limb loading) at defined speeds in walking mice and measure inter-limb phase and swing-to-stance timing to test whether transition timing shifts as the model predicts.
robot_sim: Implement four per-limb rhythm generators with load-, extension-, and balance-driven state transitions; ablate the balance signal to test for destabilized swing-to-stance transitions and wandering direction, and ablate propriospinal inter-limb coupling to reproduce speed-dependent gait changes.
